title: Catherine and Avignon
hook: the popes live in France for seventy years; a dyer's daughter urges the pope back to Rome

segments.voice: Yesterday, Julian's hazelnut, all that is made, small in her palm. Your line was kept because loved. Did your hand find the small thing in your pocket? Day eight hundred twenty-four.

The bishop of Rome, in this story, doesn't live in Rome. He lives in a great palace in Avignon, a city on the Rhône in southern France, and so did the popes before him, one after another, for many years. Rome waits. Then letters start arriving at the papal palace from a young woman in Siena. She isn't a nun in a convent, or a noblewoman, or a scholar. Her father dyes cloth for a living. And she is telling the pope, with great tenderness and no fear at all, to come home. Today: Catherine and Avignon.
screen: `THE POPE LIVES IN AVIGNON.` → `ROME WAITS.` → `LETTERS FROM SIENA.`

segments.voice: First, the situation. The popes had settled at Avignon, near the French crown, and stayed there through a long run of reigns. To Catherine, and to others in Italy, it looked as if the Church's center had drifted from the city of Peter and Paul. Second, the woman. Catherine of Siena was a laywoman who belonged to the Dominican family, wearing its habit while living at home. Tradition says she learned to read later in life, and much of what she sent out, she dictated. Her letters went to popes, kings, queens, and even captains of hired soldiers. Third, how she spoke to the pope. She called him, in her Italian, dolce Cristo in terra, sweet Christ on earth. That's not flattery; it's a title of honor and a weight. In her letters to Gregory the Eleventh, she tells him again and again to come, to return to Rome, to be a brave man and not a fearful one, and to trust God more than the voices advising delay. She even traveled to Avignon herself to tell him in person. Fourth, what happened. Gregory did go back to Rome. Historians weigh many reasons for his choice. Catherine's voice is one the Church remembers, and Catholics now honor her as a Doctor of the Church and a patron of Italy and of Europe. Her letters show a way of urging: honor and plain words, sent straight to the one who needed to hear them.
screen: `THE POPES SETTLE IN AVIGNON.` · `A DYER'S DAUGHTER FROM SIENA.` · `SWEET CHRIST ON EARTH.` · `HONOR AND PLAIN WORDS.` · then, large: `GO BACK TO ROME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: urge someone gently to do right. Settle, and bring to mind one person you care about who is putting off something they know they should do. A call they won't make. An apology. A doctor's visit. Don't rehearse a lecture. Instead, for the sit, find one sentence that has both of Catherine's halves in it: honor for who they are, and a plain word about what's next. Turn it over until it's kind and clear. If you pray, you can bring that person to God first. If you don't, just hold them warmly before you speak. The bell holds the time.
Catherine and Avignon. A dyer's daughter from Siena whose loving, fearless letters urged the pope to leave Avignon and return to Rome. Today's word.
Your line: go back to rome. Today, if the moment is right, say your one sentence to the person you thought of, kindly, plainly, and only to them. Day eight hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Catherine of Siena as a Doctor of the Church and a patron of Italy and Europe; her feast is kept in the spring, and her letters are read for their mix of tenderness and bold counsel to Church leaders.

original.note: Italian, written in the Latin alphabet: 'sweet Christ on earth,' Catherine's name for the pope in her letters.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint who scolded a pope.
what it means: a dyer's daughter who honored the pope as sweet Christ on earth and, out of that love, told him to go home.
what a scholar hears: letters dictated to Gregory the Eleventh urging courage and return, and a journey to Avignon to say it face to face.
